full_judgment:
8. Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, learned Counsel, appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-appellant,, submits that the High Court Division committed an error of law in holding that the suit is barred limitation which is based on misreading of evidence and misinterpretation of article 113 of the Limitation Act in that from pleading as well as the evidence of the plaintiff's witnesses it would appear that no time was fixed for performance of the contract and the defendant took time on different pleas to execute the deed and for the first time refused to execute the deed on 25-10-2002 and hence, the suit filed on 28-10-2002 is not barred by limitation and therefore, the judgment of the High Court Division is not sustainable in law. He further submits that the High Court Division committed an error of law in reversing the concurrent findings of the Courts below that the oral contract as well as payment of the entire consideration money have been proved by evidence and that the suit is not barred by limitation, without arriving at any specific finding of misreading or non-consideration of material evidence by the Courts below and therefore, the judgment of the High Court Division is not sustainable in law. He lastly submits that the learned Judge of the Single Bench of the High Court Division acted in excess of its revisional jurisdiction in converting itself into a third Court of facts for fresh assessment of evidence when both the Courts below on proper assessment of evidence arrived at their concurrent findings as to the proof of oral contract and payment of consideration money and therefore, the judgment of the High Court Division is not sustainable in law. 

 14. It is an acceptable proposition that in order to succeed, the plaintiff must establish his own case to obtain a decree and weakness of defendant's case is no ground for passing a decree in favour of the plaintiff. Since there was no written contract or Bainapatra between the plaintiff and the defendant No. 1 to 3 so the burden of proof heavily lies upon the plaintiff that there was existence of an oral agreement. The plaintiff Abdul Sattar while deposing as PW1 stated that defendant No. 1 rushed to his residence 28th Bhadra and the talk of selling the suit land was held in presence of witnesses, namely, Salam, Mokbul and Mostafa. He also deposed that the consideration money was settled at Taka 1,05,000 (one lac five thousand only) and he paid Taka 5,000 (five thousand only) on that day in presence of those witnesses and it was settled that the defendants would register a Kabala within 2 (two) months on receiving balance consideration money. PW1 further deposed that Nazrul pleaded an urgency to pay the balance consideration within a short while since Habibullah decided to perform Hajj with the aid of such balance consideration. He also deposed that he managed the balance consideration with a view to meet up the aforementioned emergency of Habibullah and paid such money amounting to Taka 1,00,000 (one lac) on 7th Kartik 1408 BS and Nazrul received such money in presence of Abdus Salam, Mokbul and Mustafa and at that time it was settled that Kabala would be registered after return of Habibullah from Hajj. He also deposed that soon after return of Habibullah, he insisted upon the defendant to execute a Kabala, but he took time on various pretexts. 

 22. He further adds that enforcement of the contract is a discretion of the court and exercisable on the basis of established sound evidence on record. He has relied upon a decision which has been enunciated in the case of Rezaur Rahman and others vs Ahmed Hossain Khan reported in 1986 BLD page 14 wherein it has been held that oral contract is as valid as written one but in the matter of oral contract, once it is denied by one of the parties, a heavy onus of proof lies on the other parties in establishing its truth. He lastly submits that the appellant in the instant case has adduced unimpeachable evidence upon which the court can exercise its discretion.
